sysd-blocks-035.title: Database: an organized collection of data
sysd-blocks-035.text: A flight reservation system, a parts inventory and a website built from webpages all keep their data in a database. A database is an organized collection of data, usually managed by database management software that lets users and applications capture and analyze it. Organizations rely on databases for their internal operations and for their online interactions with customers and suppliers. Strictly, the database, the software that manages it and the applications around it together form a database system. People often use the word loosely for any of the three. Databases can be classified by their contents, their application area, or a technical aspect such as structure. Some live primarily in main memory, which is faster than disk and used where response time is critical. Others spread both the data and the software over several computers. Copies protect it. Replicas of database objects give simultaneous access and resilience to partial failure. Saved copies, taken occasionally or continuously, let the database be restored after corruption or erroneous updates.

sysd-blocks-044.title: Relational database: data in tables
sysd-blocks-044.text: The relational database replaced the hierarchical and network databases before it largely because it was easier to implement and administer. It stores data in tables of columns and rows, with a unique key identifying each row. Each table generally represents one entity type, such as customer or product. Its rows are instances of that type, and its columns hold values such as address or price. Keys and normalization keep the data correct and avoid repeating it, and the model handles many-to-many relationships and supports complex queries and transactions. Many relational systems are queried with the simple language SQL. To work accurately they must use ACID transactions, described in {{ref:sysd-blocks-055}}. Singh lists the costs as expensive maintenance, difficult schema evolution, performance hits from joins, and poor horizontal scaling. A popular alternative today is {{ref:sysd-blocks-058}}, which scales horizontally across clusters of computers.

sysd-blocks-058.title: NoSQL: data without the table
sysd-blocks-058.text: NoSQL stands for "not only SQL", or simply "non-relational". A NoSQL database stores and retrieves data differently from the table structure of a relational database. Instead of rows and columns, it holds information in a single data structure such as key-value pairs, wide columns, graphs or documents. With no fixed schema, it scales easily to large, often unstructured datasets. That suits big data and real-time web applications, which value its simple design, horizontal scaling across clusters and cheap commodity hardware. The price is transactions: most NoSQL systems lack full ACID support, though some, like MongoDB, include it as a key feature. Many follow the BASE model, which trades strict consistency for speed and availability. Updates reach all nodes eventually, but reads may be stale. Barriers to adoption include low-level query languages, no ad hoc joins across tables and no standardized interfaces.

sysd-blocks-061.title: Graph database: relationships as stored links
sysd-blocks-061.text: A social network's friends relationship is essentially unbounded, and following it through tables takes join after join. A graph database stores the links themselves. It represents data with nodes for entities, edges for the relationships between them, and properties. Edges can be labeled, directed and given properties. Most systems use index-free adjacency: each node holds direct references to its neighbors instead of consulting a global index. An adjacent lookup is typically O(1) versus O(log n) for an index, so query time tracks the part of the graph touched. A relational database needs many joins for complex relationships, while a graph database follows stored links, and its advantage grows with query depth. Relational systems still suit flat data with relationships one or two levels deep, so the graph model alone should not justify a switch without evidence of gains. As of 2021 no graph query language had been adopted as universally as SQL.

sysd-blocks-059.title: Document database: one object, one document
sysd-blocks-059.text: In a document database, an object in your program becomes one record in the store. It is designed to store, retrieve and manage documents, or semi-structured information, and it is one of the main categories of NoSQL databases. A document is a self-contained unit encoded in a standard format such as XML, YAML, JSON or binary BSON. A relational database splits one object across tables joined by foreign keys. A document database keeps everything about it in one document, fetched by key without multi-table lookups. Documents need no fixed schema: those in one collection may have different fields, so new information can be added to some without affecting others. Each document has a unique identifier, and most stores index it. Beyond key access, a query language can retrieve documents by content, such as all whose field matches a value. That separates it from {{ref:sysd-blocks-060}}, which treats values as opaque. Singh counts the lack of a schema as both an advantage and a disadvantage.

sysd-q-025.title: Elasticsearch: search over large volumes of data
sysd-q-025.text: Traditional databases are sometimes not fast enough to store, search and analyze huge volumes of data in near real time, with results in milliseconds. Elasticsearch addresses that gap. It is a distributed, open search and analytics engine built on {{ref:sysd-q-093}}, with an HTTP web interface and schema-free JSON documents. Documents are stored in indices divided into primary shards, each with zero or more replicas spread across the cluster's nodes, and routing and rebalancing are automatic. One catch: once an index has been created, its number of primary shards cannot be changed. Beyond full-text search it supports faceted search, real-time search and percolation, in which stored queries are matched against incoming documents rather than the reverse. Real-time GET requests make it usable as a NoSQL datastore, though it does not support transactions that span several nodes. In a design from the System Design Primer, the search cluster is scatter-gathered: every server is asked for matches, then results are merged, ranked, sorted and returned.

sysd-blocks-060.title: Key-value store: lookup by key
sysd-blocks-060.text: One of the simplest non-trivial data models is the dictionary, a collection of key-value pairs in which each key appears at most once. A key-value store takes that model as its whole design. Every record is stored and found through its unique key. The value is opaque to the database, which typically supports only storing, retrieving, updating and deleting it by key. A document database can interpret a record's structure, but a key-value store returns a value whole. That suits low-latency, high-throughput workloads of direct key lookups, and Singh lists session management among its strengths. It is less suited to complex queries or relationships, since values cannot be filtered and there is no indexing or scanning. Variants add structure: keys kept in lexicographic order so ranges are retrieved efficiently, composite keys, or complex values such as Redis lists. Memcached and Redis hold data in memory, while Berkeley DB, Riak and Voldemort persist it.

sysd-blocks-036.title: Database management system: the software in the middle
sysd-blocks-036.text: MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle Database and Microsoft Access are all examples of one kind of software: a database management system, or DBMS. It lets users define, create, maintain and control access to a database. It sits between the database and its users or programs, letting them capture, retrieve, update and analyze data. It also provides facilities to administer the database, such as tuning and recovery. Storage, retrieval and update are the core, but what a DBMS offers beyond that varies enormously. Codd proposed that a general-purpose DBMS also provide a metadata catalog, transactions and concurrency, recovery, remote access and constraint enforcement. The database engine is the core part, between the database and the application interface. A general-purpose DBMS offers public APIs, and a special-purpose one may use a private API tied to a single application. Client-server architecture put the application on a client and the database on a server; multitier architectures later added application and web servers.

sysd-blocks-039.title: Database transaction: a unit of work, all or nothing
sysd-blocks-039.text: A bank transfer needs two steps: subtract the amount from one account and add the same amount to the other. A database transaction treats them as one. It is a unit of work performed in a database management system and handled in a coherent and reliable way, independent of other transactions. Transactions serve two purposes. They are reliable units of work that allow correct recovery from failures and keep the database consistent. They also isolate programs that access the database concurrently, because without that their outcomes are possibly erroneous. A transaction must be atomic (complete or have no effect), consistent (conform to existing constraints), isolated (not affect other transactions) and durable (written to persistent storage). Together these are abbreviated ACID, and {{ref:sysd-blocks-055}} takes them one at a time. The programmer sets a transaction's boundaries with special commands. A transaction over data on multiple nodes, covered in {{ref:sysd-scale-001}}, enforces the same guarantees, and typically an entity coordinates the process so all parts are applied everywhere.

sysd-blocks-055.title: ACID: four guarantees for every transaction
sysd-blocks-055.text:
A power failure in the middle of a bank transfer should leave no trace. ACID names four properties of database transactions that are intended to guarantee data validity despite errors, power failures and other mishaps. Relational databases follow it to keep data correct before and after a transaction.

Atomicity means all or nothing. The writes in a transaction are executed all at once and cannot be broken into smaller parts, and if a fault occurs they are rolled back. Consistency means preserving database invariants: data written by a transaction must be valid under all defined rules. This differs from the consistency meant in {{ref:sysd-scale-107}}, where every read receives the most recent write or an error. The third property, covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-040}}, keeps concurrent transactions from contending. The database moderates access so transactions appear to run sequentially, and the strictest form, serializability, makes each act as if it were the only one running. The fourth, covered in {{ref:sysd-blocks-210}}, means data stays persisted after a transaction commits, written to disk even through a system failure. In a distributed system it is replicated to other nodes.

Implementations use write-ahead logging, which writes the prospective change to a persistent log before changing the database so it can recover after a crash. The alternative is shadow paging, which applies updates to a partial copy that is activated on commit. Guaranteeing ACID across a distributed database is harder, because a network connection or another node may fail. Atomicity there comes from a protocol covered in {{ref:sysd-scale-002}}, in which a coordinator asks participants whether they are prepared before formalizing the transaction.

sysd-blocks-037.title: Database models: how data is organized logically
sysd-blocks-037.text:
Data can be organized as a table, a tree, a graph or a document, and each choice is a database model. A database model is a type of data model that determines the logical structure of a database and how its data can be stored, organized and manipulated. The most popular is the relational model, or its SQL approximation, which uses a table-based format. The list is long. Navigational, hierarchical, network, graph, relational, entity-relationship, object, document, entity-attribute-value and star schema models are all common. An object-relational database combines the object and relational structures. Others include the multidimensional, array and multivalue models. Some are specialized for particular data, such as XML, semantic and content store databases.

Three shapes show how the models differ. The flat model puts data in a single table, one record per row and one attribute per column. It is as simple as a spreadsheet but cannot efficiently handle complex relationships between entities. The hierarchical model is a tree in which each record has one parent but can have many children. It suits clear parent-child relationships but struggles with many-to-many ones and can become complex and rigid. The network model lets each record have multiple parents and children, forming a graph, and so handles many-to-many relationships efficiently.

sysd-blocks-040.title: Isolation: how much transactions see of each other
sysd-blocks-040.text: Of the four ACID properties, isolation is the one most often relaxed. It determines how a transaction's changes are visible to other users and systems. At its strictest, a transaction runs as if no others were running at the same time, a form called serializability. That is hard to implement in reality, so looser settings are often adopted. A lower level lets more users access the same data at once but increases concurrency effects such as dirty reads or lost updates. A higher level reduces those effects but needs more system resources and raises the chance that one transaction blocks another. It also makes deadlock more likely. To keep the highest isolation, a DBMS usually acquires locks on data, which can cost concurrency, or implements {{ref:sysd-blocks-054}}. Most transactions can be built to avoid levels such as SERIALIZABLE, which cuts locking overhead. The programmer must then analyze access code carefully, because relaxed isolation can cause bugs that are hard to find. The database usually enforces isolation, though a client-side transaction manager can also provide it.

sysd-blocks-045.title: Primary and foreign keys: identifying and linking rows
sysd-blocks-045.text: Every row in a table needs an identity, and the primary key supplies it. Most implementations give each row a unique primary key. A new unique value is generated when a row is written, the system uses it primarily to access the table, and performance is optimized for it. Natural attributes are sometimes good primary keys, but a surrogate key is often used instead, an artificial attribute with no intrinsic meaning, such as a student ID. Natural keys often need several columns, called a composite key, which is one reason a single integer column is usually made the primary key. A foreign key is a column that holds the primary key of a row in another table. A key that migrates to another table becomes a foreign key there, and foreign keys need not be unique. The foreign key restricts an attribute to values that exist in the referenced table, which is how tables are cross-referenced. Most designs resolve many-to-many relationships with an extra table holding the primary keys of both entity tables.

sysd-blocks-062.title: Wide-column store: rows whose columns can vary
sysd-blocks-062.text: A wide-column store looks like a relational table, but each row is free to choose its own columns. It uses tables, rows and columns, yet column names and formats can vary from row to row. It can be read as a two-dimensional key-value store, where each value is identified by two keys, a row identifier and a column identifier. Columns are grouped into column families stored together on disk, inside a top-level keyspace. A row can span several families, and a family is often likened to a relational table. The name once meant column-oriented relational databases such as C-Store. It came to mean systems that keep column families together and drop the relational model: {{ref:sysd-scale-038}}, the prototypical example, and {{ref:sysd-scale-031}}. Compared with relational databases they are denormalized, with columns added dynamically. Compared with document databases, they split records into column families that the database treats as units. Singh calls them highly scalable, able to handle petabytes, and names increased write time as a disadvantage.

sysd-blocks-051.title: OLTP and OLAP: serving users versus answering analysts
sysd-blocks-051.text:
An ATM withdrawal and a business intelligence report make opposite demands on a database. OLTP systems serve transaction-oriented applications such as order entry, retail sales, financial transactions and ATMs, and they respond to users in real time. OLAP systems answer complex analytical queries for reporting and decision support.

OLTP applications have high throughput, are insert- or update-intensive and serve hundreds of concurrent users. Their key goals are availability, speed, concurrency and recoverability. OLAP queries are much more complex and run in smaller volumes, and the workload is generally read-only. OLTP databases hold detailed, current data in normalized schemas, usually third normal form, and favor row-oriented systems. OLAP databases store aggregated, historical data in multi-dimensional schemas, usually star schemas, and benefit from column-oriented systems, because analytics usually selects specific fields rather than whole rows. OLTP performance is measured in transactions per second. OLAP has a low rate of transactions and complex queries with aggregations, so its measure is response time.

sysd-blocks-170.title: Data warehouse: a separate copy built for analysis
sysd-blocks-170.text: Long analysis queries and fast transactions fight over locks in the same database. A data warehouse ends the fight by keeping a separate copy for analysis. It is a central repository of data integrated from disparate sources and organized for reporting and analysis, used by analysts and managers to make decisions. Data from operational systems such as marketing or sales is uploaded, often cleansed first, and the warehouse stores current and historical data. Operational databases keep a snapshot of the business, while warehouses keep history and favor column-oriented storage, because analytic access selects specific fields. Warehouse data is subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and nonvolatile: it spans a long horizon, up to 10 years, and is read-only once loaded unless a regulatory obligation requires change. There are two main storage approaches. The dimensional approach (Kimball) uses star schemas, and the normalized approach (Inmon) stores third-normal-form tables grouped by subject area. A data lake instead keeps large volumes of data raw and processes it at run time.

sysd-blocks-052.title: Star and snowflake schemas: shaping warehouse data
sysd-blocks-052.text: A star schema takes its name from its shape: a fact table at the center, referencing any number of dimension tables around it. It is the simplest data mart schema style and the most widely used for warehouses. Facts hold measurable, quantitative data such as sales price, quantity, distance or weight, while dimensions hold descriptive attributes such as product models, colors, sizes, locations and salesperson names. Fact tables record metrics for specific events as numeric values plus foreign keys to dimensions, so they accumulate many rows. Dimension tables have relatively few records but many attributes each. Star schemas are denormalized: relaxing normalization gives simpler join logic, faster read-only queries and aggregations, and fewer joins per query. An analytic query usually joins one large fact table with a handful of small dimensions, as in a sales example that joins Fact_Sales to Dim_Date, Dim_Store and Dim_Product. A snowflake schema instead normalizes the dimension hierarchies into multiple linked tables. That reduces repeated data and improves integrity but needs more joins, and Kimball advises avoiding it without clear need.

sysd-blocks-168.title: Online analytical processing: slicing data cubes
sysd-blocks-168.text:
It has been claimed that OLAP cubes answer complex queries in around 0.1% of the time the same question needs on OLTP relational data. Online analytical processing is an approach to quickly answering multi-dimensional analytical queries, part of business intelligence, in which users analyze data organized in cubes interactively.

At its core is the cube: numeric facts called measures, categorized by dimensions, placed at the intersections of a hypercube and usually manipulated through a pivot-table-like interface. Its metadata is typically built from a star or snowflake schema. Three basic operations do the work. Roll-up aggregates along dimensions, such as offices up to a division. Drill-down navigates into detail, such as sales by product within a region. Slicing and dicing views a subset of the cube along other dimensions.

Aggregations, built by coarsening granularity along dimensions, are the main reason OLAP is fast. Possible aggregations are so many that usually only a predetermined number are fully calculated, and the others are solved on demand. Choosing which is the view selection problem, which is NP-complete.

sysd-blocks-176.title: Connection pooling: reusing database connections
sysd-blocks-176.text: Serverless functions can flood a database with connections. AWS Lambda opens a new database connection per invocation, which under high concurrency can cause connection storms. A proxy such as Amazon RDS Proxy pools the connections to calm them. A connection pool is a cache of reusable database connections managed by the client or middleware. Pooling reduces the overhead of opening and closing connections, which improves performance. It matters for SQL databases, which typically use stateful binary protocols that keep session information such as the state of a transaction and prepared statements. DynamoDB and Cosmos DB use stateless HTTP-based protocols, which often reduces the need. Pool settings should match the database's capacity and the workload, since overprovisioned pools cause rejected connections, throttling, resource contention and higher latency. Idle pooled connections can break through NAT timeouts, dropped connections or session invalidation, and expired login tokens can invalidate them, forcing costly reconnection. Pooling is usually done on the client side, by libraries such as ADO.NET and JDBC, not by the database engine.

sysd-blocks-038.title: Database languages: four sublanguages
sysd-blocks-038.text: A database language is a special-purpose language for working with a database, each specific to a particular data model. Four sublanguages divide the work. Data control (DCL) handles access, data definition (DDL) handles tables and relationships, data manipulation (DML) inserts, updates and deletes, and data query (DQL) searches. SQL combines definition, manipulation and query in a single language, and all mainstream commercial relational DBMSs support it with varying conformance. A database language may also configure the DBMS, compute over query results by counting, summing, averaging, sorting and grouping, and enforce constraints.

sysd-blocks-066.title: SQL: the declarative language of relational data
sysd-blocks-066.text: SQL had two advantages over older read-write APIs such as ISAM or VSAM. One command could access many records, and the programmer no longer had to specify how to reach a record, with or without an index. SQL is a domain-specific language used to manage data, especially in a relational database management system. It is set-based and declarative, not imperative like C or BASIC, though extensions add procedural features. It was among the first commercial languages to use Codd's relational model. It became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987, and despite departing from the model it became the most widely used database language. Virtually no implementation adheres fully to the standard, so most SQL code needs changes to port between systems. Date and time syntax, string concatenation, NULLs and comparison case sensitivity vary from vendor to vendor. The Null marker means the absence of a value, distinct from 0 or an empty string, and it enforces three-valued logic: true, false and unknown.

sysd-blocks-064.title: SQL vs NoSQL: a trade-off, not a contest
sysd-blocks-064.text:
Claiming that NoSQL is simply better, or that SQL is not scalable, reflects poorly in an interview, Singh warns. He treats the choice as a trade-off to settle by requirements, not as a contest with a single winner. The advice is to pick the technology that fits the requirements better.

The two kinds differ in how they are built and what they store. Relational databases are structured with predefined schemas, while non-relational ones are unstructured, distributed and have a dynamic schema. In SQL each record has a fixed schema chosen before data entry and changed only through migrations. In NoSQL fields are added on the fly and a record need not have every field. SQL is a very powerful language for defining and manipulating data, whereas NoSQL queries are focused on a collection of documents and the syntax differs between databases.

Scaling and reliability pull in different directions. SQL databases usually scale vertically, which can get very expensive, and scaling across servers is challenging. NoSQL databases scale horizontally on cheap commodity hardware, and many distribute data across servers automatically. The vast majority of relational databases are ACID compliant, so for data reliability and safe transactions SQL is still the better bet. Most NoSQL solutions sacrifice ACID compliance for performance and the ability to scale.

Pick SQL for structured data with a strict schema, relational data, complex joins, transactions and very fast lookups by index. Pick NoSQL for a flexible schema, non-relational data, no need for complex joins, a very data-intensive workload and very high throughput for IOPS.

sysd-blocks-175.title: Spatial database: points, lines and polygons
sysd-blocks-175.text: Does this city lie inside that country? In a spatial database that question is an SQL query, with a function such as ST_Contains comparing the shapes. A spatial database is a general-purpose database, usually relational, enhanced with spatial data that represents objects in a geometric space, along with tools for querying and analyzing it. Most represent points, lines and polygons, with data types mostly based on the OGC Simple Features specification. A spatial extension adds spatial datatypes that store spatial data as column values. Because locations need a spatial reference system, the database also tracks and transforms coordinate systems. Ordinary indexes sort values in a linear order, which is not optimal for queries in two or three dimensions, so a spatial index handles multi-dimensional ordering. The preferred spatial index is typically the {{ref:sysd-blocks-187}}, which groups objects by minimum bounding rectangle. Almost all current relational and object-relational DBMSs have spatial extensions. Web mapping applications need them for dynamic data that changes frequently.

sysd-blocks-169.title: MOLAP, ROLAP and HOLAP: three ways to store OLAP data
sysd-blocks-169.text:
OLAP systems are traditionally grouped by how they store data: multidimensional (MOLAP), relational (ROLAP) and hybrid (HOLAP). Vendors disagree about the specifics of each type's benefits, so treat the comparisons below as general tendencies.

MOLAP, the classic form, stores data in an optimized multi-dimensional array rather than a relational database, and often precomputes derived data such as consolidations into a data cube. It generally delivers better performance and needs less storage thanks to specialized indexing and compression. It can suffer database explosion from many dimensions, precomputed results and sparse data.

ROLAP works directly with relational databases and needs no precomputation. Base and dimension tables are relational tables, new tables hold the aggregates, and it depends on a specialized schema design. It scales better to large volumes and very high-cardinality dimensions and works with any SQL reporting tool. But it is generally slower than MOLAP, and aggregate tables need custom ETL code.

Most commercial OLAP tools now use hybrid OLAP. It lets the designer choose what sits where: aggregations in MOLAP and detail in ROLAP, or recent data in MOLAP and older data in ROLAP.

sysd-blocks-068.title: Querying and indexing in NoSQL databases
sysd-blocks-068.text: Ask a NoSQL database for a field it has not indexed and it may simply scan everything. Many run full scans for queries on non-indexed fields and apply filters after retrieving the data, though products behave differently here. Modern ones add optimizations. MongoDB supports compound indexes, Cassandra offers secondary indexes and materialized views, and Redis uses custom indexing. Elasticsearch uses {{ref:sysd-blocks-186}} for text search but can still scan non-indexed fields. These systems are designed to scale and to do key-based operations efficiently. They excel at basic CRUD and key lookups, while suitability for complex queries or joins varies.

openers.choosing-a-database: Sooner or later every design in this course has to say where its data lives. A database is an organized collection of data, usually managed by software that lets users define, create, maintain and control access to it. This chapter starts with the relational database, which stores data in tables of rows and columns, and with NoSQL, which stores and retrieves it differently, as key-value pairs, documents or graphs. It also meets the transaction, a unit of work that the four ACID properties are meant to protect against errors, power failures and other mishaps. By the end you will be able to match a kind of database to the workload it suits.
